items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose [MATH: a] is an integer, and [MATH: {\color{red}{n}}] is a positive integer. As we've seen, the division algorithm states that there exists a unique integer [MATH: q] and a unique positive integer [MATH: {\color{blue}{r}}] such that

Content:
[MATH: a = q{\color{red}{n}}+{\color{blue}{r}}, \qquad 0\leq {\color{blue}{r}} < {\color{red}{n}}.]

Content:
When two integers [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] have the same remainder [MATH: {\color{blue}{r}}] when divided by [MATH: {\color{red}{n}},] we say they are congruent modulo [MATH: \boldsymbol n,] and we write
[MATH: a\equiv b\qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).]

Content:
The number [MATH: n] is called the modulus.

Content:
To demonstrate this concretely, consider the following list of numbers:

Content:
[MATH: 1, \qquad 6, \qquad 11, \qquad 16]

Content:
These numbers are congruent modulo [MATH: \boldsymbol 5] because they each have the same remainder [MATH: ({\color{blue}{1}})] when divided by [MATH: {\color{red}{5}}.]

Content:
[MATH: 1|= 0 ⋅ 5 + 1; 6|= 1 ⋅ 5 + 1; 11|= 2 ⋅ 5 + 1; 16|= 3 ⋅ 5 + 1]

Content:
Therefore, we can write the following:

Content:
[MATH: 1|≡6|(mod5); 1|≡11|(mod5); 1|≡16|(mod5); 6|≡11|(mod5); 6|≡16|(mod5); 11|≡16|(mod5)]

Content:
Next, consider the following list of numbers:

Content:
[MATH: 2, \qquad 7, \qquad 12, \qquad 17]

Content:
These numbers are also congruent modulo [MATH: 5] because they each have a remainder of [MATH: \color{blue}{2}] when divided by [MATH: {\color{red}{5}}{:}]

Content:
[MATH: 2|= 0 ⋅ 5 + 2; 7|= 1 ⋅ 5 + 2; 12|= 2 ⋅ 5 + 2; 17|= 3 ⋅ 5 + 2]

Content:
We write this as follows:

Content:
[MATH: 2|≡7|(mod5); 2|≡12|(mod5); 2|≡17|(mod5); 7|≡12|(mod5); 7|≡17|(mod5); 12|≡17|(mod5)]

Content:
To visualize congruence modulo [MATH: 5] more generally, let's write the sequence [MATH: 0, \: 1, \: 2, \: 3, \ldots] in a spiral around a circle so that each "layer" contains exactly [MATH: 5] numbers.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3bd15cf969c3808b70954b7ac38cc2c3]

Content:
Each "spoke" of our wheel contains numbers that are congruent modulo [MATH: 5.] Every number on a given spoke is congruent modulo [MATH: 5] to every other number on that spoke.

Content:
In general, two integers [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are congruent modulo [MATH: n] if and only if [MATH: n] divides [MATH: (a-b).]
[MATH: a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b)]

Content:
We'll prove this result at the end of the lesson.

Content:
For example, the following numbers are congruent with respect to the given modulus:

Content:
- [MATH: 6\equiv 1\:(\textrm{mod}\,5)] because [MATH: 5\,\mid\, (6-1).] There is no remainder:
[MATH: (6-1)\div 5 = 5\div 5 = 1]
- [MATH: -2\equiv -8\:(\textrm{mod}\,6)] because [MATH: 6\,\mid\, \left((-2)-(-8)\right).] There is no remainder:
[MATH: \left((-2)-(-8)\right)\div 6 = 6\div 6 = 1]

Content:
However, the following numbers are not congruent with respect to the given modulus:

Content:
- [MATH: 6\not\equiv 1\:(\textrm{mod}\,4)] because [MATH: 4\,\not\mid\, (6-1).] Note that [MATH: (6-1) = 5,] which is not divisible by [MATH: 4.]
- [MATH: 0\not\equiv 13\:(\textrm{mod}\,12)] because [MATH: 12\,\not\mid\, (0-13).] Note that [MATH: (0-13) = -13,] which is not divisible by [MATH: 12.]

items.title: Identifying Congruent Integers

sections.normalized_html:
Which of the following statements are true?

  1. [MATH: 24 \equiv 12 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,3)]

  2. [MATH: 17 \equiv 21 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,4)]

  3. [MATH: 19 \equiv 12 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,9)]
sections.readable_text:
Which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: 24 \equiv 12 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,3)]
2. [MATH: 17 \equiv 21 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,4)]
3. [MATH: 19 \equiv 12 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,9)]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we recall that

[MATH: a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b).]

So, [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are congruent modulo [MATH: n] if and only if [MATH: (a-b)] is divisible by [MATH: n] (there is no remainder).

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement in turn.

  • Case I gives a true statement. Indeed, [MATH: 3 \mid (24-12).] There is no remainder: [MATH: (24-12) \div 3 = 12 \div 3 = 4]

  • Case II gives a true statement. Indeed, [MATH: 4 \mid (17-21).] There is no remainder: [MATH: (17-21) \div 4 = -4 \div 4 = -1]

  • Case III gives a false statement because [MATH: 9 \not\mid (19-12).] Notice that [MATH: 19-12 = 7,] which is not divisible by [MATH: 9.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

sections.readable_text:
Which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: -11 \equiv -29 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,6)]
2. [MATH: 90 \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,9)]
3. [MATH: -10 \equiv 4 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we recall that

[MATH: a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b).]

So, [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are congruent modulo [MATH: n] if and only if [MATH: (a-b)] is divisible by [MATH: n] (there is no remainder).

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement in turn.

  • Statement I is true because [MATH: 6 \mid (-11-(-29)).] There is no remainder: [MATH: (-11-(-29)) \div 6 = 18\div 6 = 3]

  • Statement II is true because [MATH: 9 \, | \, (90-0).] There is no remainder: [MATH: (90-0) \div 9 = 90\div 9 = 10]

  • Statement III is false because [MATH: 5 \not\mid (-10-4).] Notice that [MATH: -10-4 = -14,] which is not divisible by [MATH: 5.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

Given that [MATH: -7 \equiv 17 \,(\textrm{mod}\,n)], which of the following could be the value of [MATH: n?]

Given that [MATH: -7 \equiv 17 \,(\textrm{mod}\,n)], which of the following could be the value of [MATH: n?]

1. [MATH: n=6]
2. [MATH: n=5]
3. [MATH: n=4]

sections.normalized_html: EXPLANATION
sections.readable_text: EXPLANATION

sections.normalized_html:
First, we recall that

[MATH: a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b).]

So, [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are congruent modulo [MATH: n] if and only if [MATH: (a-b)] is divisible by [MATH: n] (there is no remainder).

We have [MATH: a-b = -7-17= -24.]

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement in turn.

  • Note that [MATH: 6 \, | \, (-24)] because [MATH: -24 \div 6 = -4,] and there is no remainder. Therefore, the statement is true when [MATH: n=6.]

  • Note that [MATH: 5 \!\not{|} \, (-24).] Therefore, the statement is false when [MATH: n=5.]

  • Note that [MATH: 4 \, | \, (-24)] because [MATH: -24 \div 4 = -6,] and there is no remainder. Therefore, the statement is true when [MATH: n=4.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

items.readable_text:
Content:
Throughout this lesson, we've been using the fact that [MATH: a] is congruent to [MATH: b] modulo [MATH: n] if and only if [MATH: n] divides [MATH: (a-b){:}]

Content:
[MATH: a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b)]

Content:
To prove this result, first note that if [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] have the same remainder [MATH: r] when divided by [MATH: n,] then by the division algorithm

Content:
[MATH: a|= pn + r; b|= qn + r]
for some integers [MATH: p] and [MATH: q.]

Content:
Subtracting the second equation from the first gives

Content:
[MATH: (a-b) = (p-q)n.]

Content:
Now, if we denote [MATH: k=p-q\in\mathbb Z,] then

Content:
[MATH: (a-b) = kn.]

Content:
So, [MATH: (a-b)] is an integer multiple of [MATH: n,] which means that [MATH: (a-b)] is divisible by [MATH: n.]

Content:
Conversely, assume that [MATH: n \mid (a-b)]. Then there is an integer [MATH: k] such that [MATH: a-b= nk.]

Content:
Now, by Euclid's division algorithm, there exist unique integers [MATH: m] and [MATH: r\in \{0, 1, \dots n-1\}] such that [MATH: b={\color{blue} n}m+\color{red}r.] Note that this means that [MATH: b \, \cong \, r \, \, (\textrm{mod} \, n).] So, we have
[MATH: a − b = nk|⟹a = b + nk; ⟹a = (nm + r) + nk; ⟹a = n(m + k) + r.]
Therefore, [MATH: a \, \equiv \, r \, \, (\textrm{mod} \, n)] and [MATH: b \, \equiv \, r \, \, (\textrm{mod} \, n),] so [MATH: a \, \equiv \, b \, \, (\textrm{mod} \, n).]

Content:
This proves that if [MATH: n] divides [MATH: (a-b)] then [MATH: a] is congruent to [MATH: b] modulo [MATH: n.]

lesson.readable_text:
Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose [MATH: a] is an integer, and [MATH: {\color{red}{n}}] is a positive integer. As we've seen, the division algorithm states that there exists a unique integer [MATH: q] and a unique positive integer [MATH: {\color{blue}{r}}] such that

Content:
[MATH: a = q{\color{red}{n}}+{\color{blue}{r}}, \qquad 0\leq {\color{blue}{r}} < {\color{red}{n}}.]

Content:
When two integers [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] have the same remainder [MATH: {\color{blue}{r}}] when divided by [MATH: {\color{red}{n}},] we say they are congruent modulo [MATH: \boldsymbol n,] and we write
[MATH: a\equiv b\qquad (\textrm{mod}\,n).]

Content:
The number [MATH: n] is called the modulus.

Content:
To demonstrate this concretely, consider the following list of numbers:

Content:
[MATH: 1, \qquad 6, \qquad 11, \qquad 16]

Content:
These numbers are congruent modulo [MATH: \boldsymbol 5] because they each have the same remainder [MATH: ({\color{blue}{1}})] when divided by [MATH: {\color{red}{5}}.]

Content:
[MATH: 1|= 0 ⋅ 5 + 1; 6|= 1 ⋅ 5 + 1; 11|= 2 ⋅ 5 + 1; 16|= 3 ⋅ 5 + 1]

Content:
Therefore, we can write the following:

Content:
[MATH: 1|≡6|(mod5); 1|≡11|(mod5); 1|≡16|(mod5); 6|≡11|(mod5); 6|≡16|(mod5); 11|≡16|(mod5)]

Content:
Next, consider the following list of numbers:

Content:
[MATH: 2, \qquad 7, \qquad 12, \qquad 17]

Content:
These numbers are also congruent modulo [MATH: 5] because they each have a remainder of [MATH: \color{blue}{2}] when divided by [MATH: {\color{red}{5}}{:}]

Content:
[MATH: 2|= 0 ⋅ 5 + 2; 7|= 1 ⋅ 5 + 2; 12|= 2 ⋅ 5 + 2; 17|= 3 ⋅ 5 + 2]

Content:
We write this as follows:

Content:
[MATH: 2|≡7|(mod5); 2|≡12|(mod5); 2|≡17|(mod5); 7|≡12|(mod5); 7|≡17|(mod5); 12|≡17|(mod5)]

Content:
To visualize congruence modulo [MATH: 5] more generally, let's write the sequence [MATH: 0, \: 1, \: 2, \: 3, \ldots] in a spiral around a circle so that each "layer" contains exactly [MATH: 5] numbers.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/3bd15cf969c3808b70954b7ac38cc2c3]

Content:
Each "spoke" of our wheel contains numbers that are congruent modulo [MATH: 5.] Every number on a given spoke is congruent modulo [MATH: 5] to every other number on that spoke.

---

Item 2 — Tutorial: Determining Congruence Using Divisibility

Content:
In general, two integers [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are congruent modulo [MATH: n] if and only if [MATH: n] divides [MATH: (a-b).]
[MATH: a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b)]

Content:
We'll prove this result at the end of the lesson.

Content:
For example, the following numbers are congruent with respect to the given modulus:

Content:
- [MATH: 6\equiv 1\:(\textrm{mod}\,5)] because [MATH: 5\,\mid\, (6-1).] There is no remainder:
[MATH: (6-1)\div 5 = 5\div 5 = 1]
- [MATH: -2\equiv -8\:(\textrm{mod}\,6)] because [MATH: 6\,\mid\, \left((-2)-(-8)\right).] There is no remainder:
[MATH: \left((-2)-(-8)\right)\div 6 = 6\div 6 = 1]

Content:
However, the following numbers are not congruent with respect to the given modulus:

Content:
- [MATH: 6\not\equiv 1\:(\textrm{mod}\,4)] because [MATH: 4\,\not\mid\, (6-1).] Note that [MATH: (6-1) = 5,] which is not divisible by [MATH: 4.]
- [MATH: 0\not\equiv 13\:(\textrm{mod}\,12)] because [MATH: 12\,\not\mid\, (0-13).] Note that [MATH: (0-13) = -13,] which is not divisible by [MATH: 12.]

---

Item 3 — Example: Identifying Congruent Integers

Example Prompt:
Which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: 24 \equiv 12 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,3)]
2. [MATH: 17 \equiv 21 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,4)]
3. [MATH: 19 \equiv 12 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,9)]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we recall that

[MATH: a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b).]

So, [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are congruent modulo [MATH: n] if and only if [MATH: (a-b)] is divisible by [MATH: n] (there is no remainder).

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Case I gives a true statement. Indeed, [MATH: 3 \mid (24-12).] There is no remainder:
[MATH: (24-12) \div 3 = 12 \div 3 = 4]
- Case II gives a true statement. Indeed, [MATH: 4 \mid (17-21).] There is no remainder:
[MATH: (17-21) \div 4 = -4 \div 4 = -1]
- Case III gives a false statement because [MATH: 9 \not\mid (19-12).] Notice that [MATH: 19-12 = 7,] which is not divisible by [MATH: 9.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

Item 6 — Example: Identifying Congruent Negative Integers

Example Prompt:
Which of the following statements are true?

1. [MATH: -11 \equiv -29 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,6)]
2. [MATH: 90 \equiv 0 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,9)]
3. [MATH: -10 \equiv 4 \quad (\textrm{mod}\,5)]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we recall that

[MATH: a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b).]

So, [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are congruent modulo [MATH: n] if and only if [MATH: (a-b)] is divisible by [MATH: n] (there is no remainder).

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Statement I is true because [MATH: 6 \mid (-11-(-29)).] There is no remainder:
[MATH: (-11-(-29)) \div 6 = 18\div 6 = 3]
- Statement II is true because [MATH: 9 \, | \, (90-0).] There is no remainder:
[MATH: (90-0) \div 9 = 90\div 9 = 10]
- Statement III is false because [MATH: 5 \not\mid (-10-4).] Notice that [MATH: -10-4 = -14,] which is not divisible by [MATH: 5.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

Item 9 — Example: Finding an Unknown Modulus

Example Prompt:
Given that [MATH: -7 \equiv 17 \,(\textrm{mod}\,n)], which of the following could be the value of [MATH: n?]

1. [MATH: n=6]
2. [MATH: n=5]
3. [MATH: n=4]

Content:
EXPLANATION

Explanation:
First, we recall that

[MATH: a \equiv b \quad (\textrm{mod}\,n) \qquad \Longleftrightarrow \qquad n \mid (a-b).]

So, [MATH: a] and [MATH: b] are congruent modulo [MATH: n] if and only if [MATH: (a-b)] is divisible by [MATH: n] (there is no remainder).

We have [MATH: a-b = -7-17= -24.]

With that in mind, let's analyze each statement in turn.

- Note that [MATH: 6 \, | \, (-24)] because [MATH: -24 \div 6 = -4,] and there is no remainder. Therefore, the statement is true when [MATH: n=6.]
- Note that [MATH: 5 \!\not{|} \, (-24).] Therefore, the statement is false when [MATH: n=5.]
- Note that [MATH: 4 \, | \, (-24)] because [MATH: -24 \div 4 = -6,] and there is no remainder. Therefore, the statement is true when [MATH: n=4.]

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and III only."

[MATH: (a-b) = (p-q)n.]
